Gulf states working on multipart peace deal to avert renewal of US-Iran war
Talks are aimed at reopening strait of Hormuz and lifting sanctions on Iran, and for Houthis to withdraw in Yemen
A multipronged peace deal to reopen the strait of Hormuz within four days of sanctions being lifted and for the Houthis to withdraw substantial forces inside Yemen are at the heart of Gulf states’ plans to avert what they regard as a disastrous renewal of war between Iran and the US.
The US is aware of the talks’ progress but is holding out for a concession that European powers suggest could involve Iran allowing UN weapons inspectors back into the country.
The British foreign secretary, Ed Miliband, urged the Iranians to agree to readmit the UN weapons inspectors when he met the Iranian foreign minister, Abbas Araghchi, in New York but so far Iran has refused, saying it will only hold talks in principle on its nuclear programme.
Oil price rises above $117 a barrel amid fears US will renew strikes on Iran
European diplomats believe allowing weapons inspectors to reenter Iran and visit its bombed nuclear sites is a minimum requirement for a breakthrough with the US president, Donald Trump.
But Iran remains focused solely on the guarantees of sanctions relief it would receive in return for reopening the strait of Hormuz . Dr Ali Bagheri, the deputy secretary of Iran’s national security council, said Iran was willing to reduce its proposal that the strait reopen seven days after economic sanctions are lifted to four days.
In a further sign of flexibility, Iran is starting to acknowledge it has a mediating role in the parallel conflict in Yemen . Iran’s secretary of the supreme national security council, Mohsen Rezaei, met the Houthi’s ambassador to Iran, Ibrahim al-Dulaimi, on Tuesday.
The meeting took place 24 hours after a high-level delegation from Saudi Arabia, Turkey and Pakistan travelled to Tehran to discuss Saudi terms for ending the Yemen conflict as well as a longer-term security architecture for the region.
Iran backs the Houthis, and has the power to influence them, including devising proposals that stop short of a Houthi military victory that many say is unobtainable. In return the Houthis are demanding that Saudi Arabia lift what it regards as a naval and air blockade on Houthi-held territory.
Iran successfully prevented discussion of its nuclear programme at the meeting with Turkey, Saudi Arabia and Pakistan, and instead ensured the focus was a broader discussion about a long-term regional security vision that would include the Gulf states and Iran and see the US presence in the Middle East reduced or ended.
A new non-aggression pact in which Iran is no longer ostracised by the rest of the Gulf, as it has been since the 1979 Islamic Revolution, would meet Iran’s highest strategic goal.
An agreed commitment to this goal by six Gulf states might also make it easier for Iran to swallow potentially difficult tactical concessions that it would be required to make concerning its nuclear programme.
US and Israel are warned against launching fresh strikes on Iran
One of the key advocates of the inclusive security plan, Oman’s foreign minister, Badr Albusaidi , said he believed the US administration understood this was the direction the region is heading.
He said: “I think if Iran is fully re-engaged in this idea of having all of us, eight countries at peace with the rest of the world, the economic potential is going to be enormous for all of us in the region and those outside the region who choose to take part in this development. We have really discussed this in at length during the talks between Iran and the United States, and I think there is general acceptance that this will be the direction of travel once we have a deal in place at the end of the day.”
At a televised event in Iran this week Araghchi underlined the importance of a new postwar security pact to Iran, saying: “Recently, there has been talk of a new war but I am already thinking about the postwar period. Whether there is war or not, our policies remain the same.”

Trump says Iran war will end 'when I want it to' as costs balloon
Trump said it "would be very quick, but we have to have an end properly," with a "total statement" that Iran would never have a nuclear weapon.
His statement comes as a report from The Hill revealed that the costs of the Iran conflict have ballooned to $47 billion.
The war is costing American families about $2,000 more since it started, according to Mark Zandi, chief economist at Moody's Analytics.
US President Donald Trump speaks to the media before boarding Air Force One at Joint Base Andrews, Maryland on Oct. 27, 2026.
U.S. President Donald Trump has reiterated his claim that the Iran war will end "whenever I want it to," but insists that Tehran cannot have a nuclear weapon.
Speaking at a rally in Lubbock, Texas, Trump said "Somebody asked me before, 'When will the war in Iran end?' I said, 'Whenever I want it to end.'"
Trump said it "would be very quick, but we have to have an end properly ," with a "total statement" that Iran would never have a nuclear weapon.
His statement comes as the president grapples with poll numbers that are near a record low due to rising energy costs and affordability issues as the U.S. heads into the midterm elections on Nov. 3.
Currently, Trump's approval ratings stand at 32%, according to a Reuters/Ipsos poll on Monday.
Mark Zandi, chief economist at Moody's Analytics, said on Oct. 12 that the war was costing American families an average of $2,000 so far, where $1,100 comes from higher energy costs, $540 from heightened interest rate costs and $360 due to increased military spending.
The Iran conflict shows no sign of winding down, with Trump saying that he will soon decide whether to "make a deal" with Iran or "finish it off."
Earlier in the month, the U.S. had evacuated diplomats from Saudi Arabia, as The New York Times reported that U.S. and Israeli militaries have drawn up specific plans for a "short but intensive" operation for strikes on Iran after the midterm elections.
An estimate by U.S. Central Command on Oct. 16, according to a report by The Hill, also revealed that the cost of the Iran war has ballooned to $47 billion, about $3 billion more than the previous numbers.
The bulk of the costs was reportedly for munitions replacements at $29 billion. Washington's conflict with Iran has caused "shortfalls" in U.S. munitions, despite Trump claiming on Sept. 3 that the U.S. had "virtually unlimited" amounts of ammunition.
The massive price tag on the war does not include the costs of damaged military bases in the Middle East, which is estimated at $184 million as of June 29, according to a lead inspector general report to Congress.
This figure counts damage to U.S. diplomatic facilities in four countries — Iraq, Kuwait, Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates — from Iranian strikes.
Correction: The bulk of the costs was reportedly for munitions replacements at $29 billion. An earlier version misstated the figure.

items.content:
UK vows defense spending will hit 3% of GDP by 2030
The U.K. set 2030 as the target for defense spending to reach 3% of GDP, while reaffirming it would meet the NATO commitment of 3.5% by 2035.
Finance minister John Healey announced an additional £10 billion in economic and military support for Ukraine, as well as urgent winter military funding.
Healey also outlined up to £5 billion for defense and dual-use investment and a £2.5 billion Rolls-Royce turbine technology partnership.
Britain's Chancellor of the Exchequer John Healey holds the red Budget box outside 11 Downing Street ahead of the announcement of the Autumn Budget in the House of Commons in London, United Kingdom on October 28, 2026.
Wiktor Szymanowicz | Future Publishing | Getty Images
The U.K. has set out a target date for defense spending to rise to 3% of GDP, as the finance minister announced billions in aid for Ukraine in a "clear message to Moscow".
John Healey on Wednesday set a target date of 2030 for the 3% figure, while reaffirming its NATO commitment to reach 3.5% by 2035 .
Healey, who resigned as defense minister under the previous government over insufficient spending, presented his first annual budget as finance minister and highlighted a "new era of threat".
"Today we send a clear message to Moscow: Britain will stand with Ukraine for as long as it takes," he said as he announced an additional £10 billion ($13.3 billion) in economic and military support, based on loans, export finance guarantees, as well as £500 million in urgent military funding for this winter.
The government will set out the details of how it will meet its defense spending targets at the spending review next year, Healey told lawmakers.
"As we look ahead to the spending review, we start from a position of strength, with spending at that higher base, there will be choices we have to make about priorities," he said.
"Today, I'm getting work underway to get there in a fiscally sustainable way," Healey said against the backdrop of strained public finances and increasing borrowing costs.
‘Project Firepower’: Inside Rheinmetall’s gunpowder expansion as Europe races to replenish its ammunition
Europe’s defense boom faces a new test: Can it actually deliver weapons?
Ukraine’s drone playbook is wreaking havoc in Russia — and upending where NATO wants to invest
Tank maker KNDS postpones IPO amid market struggles for defense
Defense stocks plummet on reports Germany is scrapping warships; Rheinmetall stock down 18%
Healey also said the National Wealth Fund and British Business Bank will deploy up to £5 billion over the next four years into defence, dual-use technologies and other sectors supporting national security to strengthen the UK defense industrial base, support domestic supply chains and attract private investment.
Chris Beauchamp, chief UK market analyst at investing and trading platform IG, said Healey's announcement lacked detail but "it looks like defence will get the money Healey said was needed when he was defence secretary."
"The precise path will come through next year, but it seems like the spending bonanza for Rolls-Royce and others is still on the way. It just might take a little while to arrive," he added.
Healey also announced that Rolls-Royce will develop its next-generation turbine engine technology in partnership with the U.K. government, in an investment worth £2.5 billion.

Ukraine war briefing: Kyiv retaking territory, Zelenskyy says, as Nordic leaders urge Putin to end the conflict
Ukrainian president says Kyiv’s battlefield ⁠position strongest ⁠in some ​time. What we know on day 1,708
Volodymyr Zelenskyy has said Ukrainian forces are retaking territory through a series of offensives , adding Kyiv’s battlefield ⁠position was the strongest it had been ⁠in some ​time. The Ukrainian president, citing ⁠a report by senior commanders, noted for the first time the “Veles” operation using pipelines in Ukraine’s northeast. He also referred to an air assault operation in ⁠eastern Ukraine and the “Vivaldi” operation further to the north, designed to prevent Russian advances in ​key areas.
The leaders of Finland and Norway phoned Russian president Vladimir Putin on Tuesday to urge him to end the war in Ukraine. The call by Finnish president Alexander Stubb and Norwegian prime minister Jonas Gahr Stoere was an attempt to ⁠influence the diplomatic process after US president Donald ⁠Trump stunned allies by agreeing to buy Russian diesel, plunging ties with Ukraine to their lowest point in 18 months.
While a localised ceasefire appears to holding in Ukraine’s south, Russian strikes damaged a university campus and Kyiv’s important Southern Bridge overnight , in what Zelenskyy described as “a serious escalation” against ​Ukrainian logistics. A Ukrainian military source told Reuters that Russia ‌had hit the bridge with four Iskander ​ballistic missiles. Zelenskyy said energy facilities, logistics and infrastructure in ​10 other regions had also been attacked overnight.
Kyiv plans to allocate 1 billion hryvnias ($22 ⁠million) to build water crossings over the River Dnipro that divides ⁠the capital into two ⁠parts , ​the city’s mayor has said, as Russia escalates its attacks on ⁠bridges.
Romanian president Nicusor Dan has called an alleged Russian sabotage plot last month a “grave violation” of the Nato member’s sovereignty and security . Dan’s remarks on Tuesday came a day after the Romanian intelligence service said it identified a Russia-coordinated “sabotage network” linked to a fire in central Brasov County last month, which damaged the premises of several commercial entities. Three foreign nationals – two Belarusians and one Ukrainian, all residing in EU countries – were being investigated in connection with the fire. Romania’s foreign ministry said on Tuesday it had summoned Russia’s ambassador in Bucharest. The Russian embassy in Romania said its ambassador rejected the “baseless” accusations.
France has temporarily relocated a maritime patrol aircraft to ⁠Romania to help identify navigation dangers and bolster the protection of critical energy infrastructure ⁠in the Black ⁠Sea. At least eight cargo ships have been hit ⁠near the coast Romania and Bulgaria in the past three weeks, ⁠with about 34 sailors reported dead or missing. Romania’s defence ministry said on Tuesday the purpose is “to identify dangers to navigation and increase the ability to protect critical infrastructure in Romania’s exclusive ⁠economic zone”.
Poland will host a maintenance centre for the US-made Patriot air-defence system. The centre in Poland will be the only one outside the US, deputy defence minister Sobkowiak-Czarnecka said on social media. Poland, a Nato member bordering Ukraine, serves as a major logistics hub for military aid sent by Kyiv’s allies. Patriot interceptor missiles are regarded as among Ukraine’s most important air-defence assets as it seeks to repel escalating Russian missile and drone attacks.
Pope Leo XIV’s chief almsgiver, Monsignor Luis Marín de San Martín, on Tuesday began a three-day visit to Ukraine and was bringing several trucks worth of winter clothes, blankets and food to Kyiv for distribution. Marín de San Martín was planning to visit the capital, Zaporizhzhia, Dnipro and Fastiv, Vatican News said. Leo had called for a ceasefire and the delivery of food and medicine in Oleshky, and the safe and voluntary evacuation of its people during a phone calls with Putin and Zelenskyy.

items.title: Microsoft Maia 300: Could Its New AI Chip Challenge NVIDIA? - Cloud Wars
items.summary: Microsoft Maia 300: Could Its New AI Chip Challenge NVIDIA?  Cloud Wars
items.content:
In today’s Cloud Wars Minute, I analyze Microsoft’s ambitious Maia 300 rollout and how owning its own AI chips could give the company greater control over its AI infrastructure, improve efficiency, and reduce its reliance on NVIDIA.
00:10 — Microsoft has announced Maia 300 , the company's latest custom AI chip. It's also revealed plans to expand its Azure Maia systems to multi-gigawatt deployments starting in 2027, and with this rollout, Maia will become the primary AI inference system for Microsoft products and services.
01:02 — Microsoft expects Maia 300 to deliver 40% more tokens per megawatt than leading GPU-based systems. In other words, Microsoft expects to deliver more AI output for the same amount of power. That's crucial as demand for AI services continues to skyrocket. Now, Microsoft also says that in a full configuration, Maia 300 systems are expected to deliver up to seven times the rack-scale token throughput of Maia 200.
01:41 — Bear in mind that Maia 200 is already a very capable system, and Maia 300 really builds on those foundations — I'm going to quote Microsoft here: "To enable more coding with GitHub, more flexible AI model deployment through Microsoft Foundry, and faster interactions with Copilot, Teams, and Dragon Copilot." Now, back to that incredibly important point I made at the start.
02:05 — Maia is set to become the primary AI inference system for Microsoft products and services. Now, back in August, I talked about what this could mean for NVIDIA. My conclusion was that Microsoft's own chips could help level the playing field and give the company more options.
02:33 — Could Microsoft chips potentially challenge NVIDIA in the market? I think that remains to be seen. Microsoft's announcement certainly seems to suggest that it will have more control over its AI infrastructure , but it doesn't necessarily mean that NVIDIA is being pushed out of the picture altogether. What is clear, though, is that Microsoft is moving towards a much more full-circle AI business with its own chips, cloud infrastructure, models, and applications.

items.title: OpenAI Is Buying Google’s AI Chips, a Hit to Nvidia’s Biggest Customer Bond - 24/7 Wall St.
items.summary: OpenAI Is Buying Google’s AI Chips, a Hit to Nvidia’s Biggest Customer Bond  24/7 Wall St.
items.content:
OpenAI Is Buying Google’s AI Chips, a Hit to Nvidia’s Biggest Customer Bond
OpenAI reportedly buying Google's custom AI chips would quietly shift leverage in one of the most lucrative vendor relationships in tech, and the fallout for NVIDIA's pricing power and Alphabet's chip ambitions is only beginning to take shape.
The symbolic act of connecting to an AI processing unit highlights the critical role of specialized chips in advancing artificial intelligence, mirroring the recent strategic shifts in the tech industry. © 24/7 Wall St.
OpenAI has spent more on NVIDIA ( NASDAQ:NVDA | NVDA Price Prediction ) graphics processors than almost any other company, and it now plans to buy Google's own AI chips, according to The Information. The report came out the night of October 27, 2026. It cites one person familiar with the matter and mentions Google's tensor processing units (TPUs), custom chips built for AI work.
Neither company has confirmed the plan. Google did not immediately respond to a request for comment, and OpenAI declined to comment.
Alphabet  ( NASDAQ:GOOG , NASDAQ:GOOGL ) closed at $320.58, up 1.19%, a gain of $3.78, and then added 0.93% after hours to reach $323.57. NVIDIA rose 0.9% to $217.94 and stayed nearly flat after hours at $218.14.
No terms, volumes, timing, or chip generation have been disclosed. Until one of the companies confirms it, this remains a reported plan, since nobody has shown a signed order.
OpenAI has used TPUs before. It began renting Google's AI chips in June 2025, and the report adds that it now owns them. A year earlier, OpenAI said it had "no specific plans to use TPUs at present."
OpenAI has been moving in this direction for a while. It recently said it would offer its frontier models through Google Cloud. In June, it announced its first custom chip, and a current job listing asks for "significant experience optimizing real workloads on TPUs for training or inference."
A buyer this large wants a second supplier because it gains leverage on price, protection against supply shortages, and software that is not tied to a single vendor.
Alphabet started selling TPUs directly to some customers this year, although its chief financial officer has said most of that revenue will be recognized in 2027. Google already rents TPUs to Anthropic, Apple ( NASDAQ:AAPL ) and Citadel Securities. An OpenAI purchase would show that TPUs can work as a chip business selling to outside buyers, on top of a cloud unit whose revenue grew 82% to $24.77 billion last quarter.
For NVIDIA, the first measure is scale: its data center unit brought in $89.02 billion in a single quarter. Its financial ties to OpenAI are also extensive. On August 17, 2026, NVIDIA agreed to provide up to $105 billion in credit support for an OpenAI data center in Ohio that starts at 4.25 gigawatts. NVIDIA CEO Jensen Huang reportedly said OpenAI committed to spend about $600 billion on NVIDIA servers through 2030.
OpenAI still calls itself one of NVIDIA's biggest customers. On the same day as the report, its computing chief said, in a joint announcement with NVIDIA and Oracle ( NYSE:ORCL ), "We are bringing Vera into production on OCI to support these workloads at scale."
Huang has said he is "very confident that they're going to be customers and partners of ours for a very long time." As the seller, he would naturally say that, but no evidence shows OpenAI cutting its orders.
The risk to NVIDIA is a slow loss of pricing power, because each credible alternative improves the buyer's position in negotiations. NVIDIA trades at a price-to-earnings ratio of 44, and that multiple assumes NVIDIA keeps its 71.1% gross margin. TPU software still lags behind NVIDIA's, so the purchase could be smaller or slower than the headline implies.
Alphabet has fallen 5.79% over the past week and is up only 2.62% this year, while NVIDIA is up 17.13%.
At a P/E of 14 and a market value of $3.874 trillion, Alphabet costs far less than NVIDIA at $5.263 trillion. That gap suggests the market gives little premium to Alphabet's position as a credible second AI chip supplier.
The next test comes when Alphabet reports after the close on October 28, 2026. If management names outside TPU buyers or raises its 2027 TPU revenue outlook, the case gets stronger. If the call skips TPUs and the stock closes below $320.58, the market will have viewed this report as noise.

items.content:
North Korean flags in Pyongyang. Kim Won Jin / AFP via Getty
The United States issued new North Korea-related sanctions on Wednesday, targeting 10 individuals and one entity, according ⁠to a notice posted to the Treasury Department’s website.
The Treasury Department said the schemes involve North Korean IT workers fraudulently gaining employment with companies in the United States and elsewhere, and Pyongyang taking most of the workers’ wages to fund its weapons of mass ⁠destruction and ballistic missile programs.
“These networks permeate ​through ⁠the global financial system, necessitating a unified response to match the threat,” the department said in a statement, adding that ⁠Australia and the European Union also imposed North Korea-related sanctions this month.
North ​Korea’s ⁠mission to the United Nations ‌in New York did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
The sanctions come ‌as President Donald Trump has been eager to jump-start talks with North Korea, but ‌Pyongyang has shown little interest in ‌diplomacy aimed at containing its nuclear program. However, earlier this month Trump downplayed the idea of another high-profile ⁠meeting with Kim in China next month.
Trump became the only U.S. president to have met a North Korean leader when he held an unprecedented series of summits with Kim in 2018 and 2019, but the diplomatic efforts ‌broke down over US demands that North ​Korea give up its nuclear weapons.

items.content:
China Is Building Its Way Around Europe’s EV Tariffs
Beijing’s evolving industrial playbook is taking shape in Morocco.
By Aaron Glasserman , a distinguished fellow at the Weatherhead East Asian Institute at Columbia University and a fellow on foreign policy at the Asia Society Policy Institute’s Center for China Analysis, and Jessie Jiexi Lin , a student pursuing a master’s in public administration at Columbia University’s School of International and Public Affairs.
Workers in dark uniforms and blue baseball caps inspect the metal frames of silver, unpainted electric vehicles along a brightly lit assembly line on a factory floor. The line of cars extends backward to the far wall, with similar small groups of workers bustling around each one.
Workers check vehicle frames on the production line for electric vehicle maker Zeekr at its factory in Ningbo, China, on May 29, 2025. Kevin Frayer/Getty Images
In recent years, Europe’s auto industry has reeled from the influx of low-cost, high-quality Chinese electric vehicles (EVs). Even as Brussels imposes tariffs on Chinese-made EVs, their market share only continues to grow. As of December, more than 9 percent of all new automobiles sold in Europe were made in China, with some estimates expecting Chinese EVs to account for roughly 20 percent of the Western European market by 2028.
Brussels’s retaliatory tariffs reflect a common Western view that high-value Chinese products are competitive in global markets largely because of state subsidies . To be sure, China’s EV industry has benefited immensely from Beijing’s subsidies, easy credit, and tax relief. That explanation, however, is far too narrow and risks severely underestimating the scale of the challenge ahead.
In recent years, Europe’s auto industry has reeled from the influx of low-cost, high-quality Chinese electric vehicles (EVs). Even as Brussels imposes tariffs on Chinese-made EVs, their market share only continues to grow. As of December, more than 9 percent of all new automobiles sold in Europe were made in China, with some estimates expecting Chinese EVs to account for roughly 20 percent of the Western European market by 2028.
Brussels’s retaliatory tariffs reflect a common Western view that high-value Chinese products are competitive in global markets largely because of state subsidies . To be sure, China’s EV industry has benefited immensely from Beijing’s subsidies, easy credit, and tax relief. That explanation, however, is far too narrow and risks severely underestimating the scale of the challenge ahead.
The more consequential story—that will likely make Chinese EVs even more competitive in the near future—is Beijing’s evolving approach to overseas industrial policy. At the core of this approach is an increasingly coordinated model of public- and private-sector activity.
State-owned enterprises (SOE) lay the groundwork for favorable investment environments abroad by undertaking massive infrastructure projects and securing access to strategic resources. Boosted by Beijing’s diplomatic ties and international clout, private companies leverage these state-backed platforms as a springboard for trade by bringing in investment, production capacity, and industry-specific expertise.
The advantages of this approach for Beijing—and the challenge that it poses to foreign companies—are already on full display in Morocco, where years of existing strategic investment, infrastructure development, and geopolitical maneuvering are pushing China closer to vertically integrating EV supply chains, bypassing tariffs, and further reshaping Europe’s auto industry.
It is only in recent years that Morocco has emerged as a key node in China’s EV empire.
For decades, Beijing maintained much closer ties with Morocco’s neighbor and rival, Algeria, but that began to change in the early 2010s as the Belt and Road Initiative (BRI) took off. In 2016, Morocco joined the growing ranks of countries signing “strategic partnerships” with China, making mutual commitments to expand economic cooperation and recognize each other’s core interests.
The next year, Morocco officially entered the BRI, and China has since poured millions of dollars into Morocco’s energy and transportation sectors . Almost a decade later, that economic relationship has expanded dramatically: In March, China’s committed investment in the country exceeded $10 billion , concentrated mostly in the EV and energy sectors.
China’s EV manufacturing capacity in Morocco builds on years of large-scale, state-backed investment in transportation infrastructure and natural resources. Over the past decade, Chinese SOEs have collaborated on major infrastructure and development projects in Morocco, including bridges , highways , and smart cities . Some of these are directly relevant to the EV industry, such as the chemical processing unit in Khouribga, home to one of the world’s biggest reserves of phosphate, which is critical for EV battery production .
This SOE-led scramble for resources and construction-heavy projects paved the way for private Chinese companies in the EV sector to establish footholds in Morocco and ship to overseas markets. Tanger Tech City, China’s SOE-led flagship collaboration with Morocco, is located less than 30 miles from Tanger Med, the largest container port in Africa. Taking advantage of no-fee business registration and tax-free dividends, private Chinese companies—including the global battery giant BTR New Material Group as well as tire manufacturers Sentury Tire and Guizhou Tyre—have established or announced plans to establish production bases in the industrial zone.
Elsewhere in the country, major private investments include battery manufacturer Gotion’s $1.3 billion factory and a $2 billion joint-venture battery materials factory between China’s CNGR Advanced Material and the Moroccan private equity firm Al Mada.
This isn’t to deny the role of subsidies and preferential financing, which Beijing sees as key tools for supporting companies that are expanding internationally. A 2024 directive , for instance, called on Chinese financial institutions to improve credit approval and lending procedures and to enhance cross-border settlement to “better support companies expanding into international markets.” Closer collaboration among Chinese banks, semi-official trade organizations, and Moroccan banks has also helped to streamline financing and channel investment into the African market.
But these policies are useful to Chinese firms because they are operating in an industrial landscape that SOEs have already shaped, with relatively easy access to necessary resources and infrastructure.
China’s success with this approach has only been possible because it also advances Rabat’s desire to expand domestic manufacturing capability and position Morocco as Africa’s next industrial powerhouse. Chinese investment is expected to generate sorely needed jobs; Morocco’s unemployment rate has hardly dipped below 10 percent for the past decade, and youth unemployment in cities stands at a staggering 47 percent. Officials claim that the Gotion factory alone will create 17,000 local jobs, including 2,300 high-skilled positions.
Beijing has coupled this economic engagement with a subtle diplomatic shift in favor of Rabat’s claims over Western Sahara . For decades, China has avoided explicitly backing either Morocco or Western Sahara, though its rhetoric often leaned toward the latter—and thus to the latter’s main sponsor, Algiers . With one exception in 2018, it consistently voted in favor of United Nations Security Council resolutions extending the peacekeeping mission in Western Sahara and affirming support for the Sahrawi people’s right to self-determination.
However, in recent years, China has done an about-face. In 2024, its Ministry of Foreign Affairs implicitly acknowledged the importance of the Western Sahara question for Rabat, stating , “China supports Morocco in maintaining national security and stability and is ready to work with Morocco to continue firmly supporting each other on issues concerning their respective core interests.” Then, last fall, Beijing abstained on the most recent U.N. resolution on the matter, which for the first time endorsed Rabat’s proposal to formally establish Western Sahara as an autonomous region under Moroccan sovereignty.
The full payoff of China’s Moroccan gambit will materialize if and when localized EV manufacturing matures, which could take years. That is still a tall order, as evidenced by the recent shelving of a BYD assembly plant project that had been stalled since 2017 due to budget issues and limited local charging infrastructure, according to a company executive.
Though Chinese automakers are not yet building assembly plants in Morocco, the country matters for everything “upstream” of assembly. It is becoming an integrated ecosystem for the production of batteries, tires, and other components, which reduces Chinese EV companies’ reliance on direct shipments from China and lowers costs for Chinese assembly plants in Europe and Africa.
Morocco also offers Chinese firms convenient access to the European market through the Tanger Med port and—more importantly—a rules-based pathway through Brussels’s tightening trade defenses . Currently, the EU imposes duties of up to 35 percent on EVs manufactured in China. However, vehicles that qualify as Moroccan in origin can enter the European market duty-free. That includes vehicles assembled in Morocco, so long as foreign parts make up less than 45 percent of the finished vehicle’s ex-works price.
In short, if Chinese EV companies succeed in establishing vehicle assembly factories and fully integrating supply chains in Morocco, they will be able to sell vehicles to Europe under a “Made in Morocco” label, avoiding both the 10 percent EU standard automobile tariff and the additional punitive tariff on Chinese-made EVs—reducing the total tariff effect from as much as 45 percent to zero. This would pose an unprecedented threat to what remains one of the EU’s most important industries .
China is rolling out this coordinated approach to overseas industrial policy elsewhere to varying degrees.
In Thailand, for example, China is a key investor in the Eastern Economic Corridor, a flagship regional development initiative anchored by a high-speed railway that will connect several Thai cities and seaports to China. The corridor has, in turn, provided an attractive environment for private Chinese investment. China is now the corridor’s largest source of foreign direct investment, primarily in the EV sector and related industries. Like Tanger Tech City, the corridor offers private Chinese companies major tax incentives and more convenient access to the Association of Southeast Asian Nations’ market.
The United Arab Emirates offers another example. In 2017, Chinese SOE Jiangsu Provincial Overseas Cooperation and Investment Company Limited (JOCIC) partnered with Abu Dhabi Ports to develop an industrial and special economic zone inside the Khalifa Port’s free trade zone. JOCIC set up a wholly owned UAE subsidiary to manage the park, which lets it attract Chinese private capital while insulating the parent company from project-level and geopolitical risk. The park’s location provides Chinese companies with a convenient base for expansion into the Persian Gulf and wider Middle Eastern markets, along with exemptions from value-added tax and other financial incentives . As of 2025, more than 40 Chinese companies had collectively committed more than $700 million to the park, with a focus on EVs and renewable energy.
Beijing has long seen its SOEs as tools for advancing its broader economic interests. As China in recent years has emphasized “small and beautiful” projects , the SOE-led megaprojects are often viewed as commercially disappointing holdovers from an earlier and more profligate era of BRI. Nevertheless, under this coordinated strategy, Beijing has been able to capitalize on the advantages secured by past infrastructure projects and deepen its presence in the overseas market.
As governments in industrialized economies respond to China’s surge of high-value manufactured exports, they must recognize how the sources of Chinese firms’ advantages are changing. Today, those advantages come not just from subsidies and cheap credit at home but also from integrated ecosystems abroad, built through coordination between public and private enterprise.
This means that Brussels’s retaliatory tariffs and the recently announced limits on hybrid EVs imported from China, on their own, are unlikely to stem the tide of EVs made by Chinese firms operating around the world. China’s rivals—even in industrialized economies—will struggle to compete unless they can coordinate across borders and build supply chains and infrastructure that leverage or, far less plausibly, completely sidestep what China has already put in place.
Aaron Glasserman is a distinguished fellow at the Weatherhead East Asian Institute at Columbia University and a fellow on foreign policy at the Asia Society Policy Institute’s Center for China Analysis.
Jessie Jiexi Lin is a student pursuing a master’s in public administration at Columbia University’s School of International and Public Affairs.

Rescue workers at the site of Wednesday’s rail disaster in Spain’s Toledo province. A high-speed service hit another train halted by a signalling fault. Photograph: Burak Akbulut/Anadolu/Getty Images
Rescue workers at the site of Wednesday’s rail disaster in Spain’s Toledo province. A high-speed service hit another train halted by a signalling fault. Photograph: Burak Akbulut/Anadolu/Getty Images
Second fatal train collision this year casts doubt over Spain’s high-speed rail network
Questions were raised before Toledo crash over rail safety in a country where train travel has surged by 40%
Spain’s high-speed rail network, the most extensive in Europe and the second largest in the world after China, has long ranked as a point of pride in the country. But Wednesday’s deadly crash – the second in nine months – has recast the spotlight on questions about safety.
Officials said at least 64 people were killed on Wednesday morning after two trains collided, leading to the derailment of several carriages. The two trains were carrying 544 passengers.
While the cause of the accident has yet to be confirmed, a source told Reuters that a train operated by the private company Iryo had come to a halt near the city of Toledo because of a signalling fault and on orders from infrastructure manager Adif. Soon after, a second train, operated by state-owned Renfe struck the stationary train. It had been travelling on the same line at a high speed.
Renfe said in a statement that its train had been instructed to continue on its way and had crashed into ​the stationary Iryo train “for reasons we don’t know”.
The accident follows a crash in January that killed 46 people and left dozens more injured near the town of Adamuz in Andalucía.
A Guardia Civil officer collects evidence at the site of January’s fatal rail crash near Adamuz in Andalucía. Photograph: Manu Fernández/AP Media on Wednesday were swift to point to the parallels between the two crashes: both involved the same train operators and took place on the line connecting Madrid to the southern region of Andalusia, which is the oldest on Spain’s high-speed network.
The first crash sparked a wider conversation over safety on the line, a debate that rail unions say has continued.
Wednesday’s disaster came a day before a planned 24-hour work stoppage at Renfe by Spain’s largest train drivers union. “Our goal is to change the system and make it safer,” the union said earlier this month.
Their reasons for taking action ranged from the need for climate emergency protocols to ensuring channels of communication for workers to convey concerns. The union also called for guarantees that trains would be “reliable and safe”, adding: “We demand real and definitive technical solutions to the safety and reliability issues that have long plagued our rolling stock.”
map It has also called a rolling, six-day strike for drivers at the high-speed rail operator Ouigo.
The January crash sparked a bout of political finger-pointing over whether Pedro Sánchez’s Socialist party government had spent enough on railway maintenance in a country where travel by train accounts for about 57% of all transport.
Train travel grew by 40% from 2019 to 2024, coinciding with a period in which the country opened up its rail network to private companies. In the first half of this year, 25 million passengers used a high-speed train in Spain.
The government says it has increased spending on railway network maintenance by 54% since taking power in 2018.
The aftermath of the 2013 crash near Santiago de Compostela that claimed 80 lives. It remains Spain’s worst rail disaster. Photograph: Reuters Spain spends more than any other country on its high-speed network, averaging about €1.5bn (£1.26bn) a year from 2018 to 2022, according to a Reuters analysis of EU data. More than 90% of Spain’s train network is equipped with the highest level of safety control systems in the EU.
Much of the funding, however, has seemingly been directed at new infrastructure, with about 16% earmarked for maintenance, renewal and upgrades.
Data from the European Commission suggests Spain’s maintenance investment in its 4,000km (2,500 miles) of high-speed lines has lagged behind countries such as Germany or Switzerland although some of this could be attributed to differences in the age of the rail lines and the cost of public works and materials.
Until this year, Spain had among the lowest accident rates in the EU, with just one or fewer fatalities per thousand kilometres of track, according to data from Eurostat, the statistics arm of the EU.
Spain’s worst rail accident took place in 2013, when 80 people died after a train veered off a curved section of track outside the north-western city of Santiago de Compostela.

A ceasefire that began with the aim of getting food and medicine to the Russian-occupied Ukrainian city of Oleshky has been extended across the wider southern region of Kherson, according to sources.
Several thousand residents are trapped in the city with no access to food, water and electricity. On one side is the Dnipro river, while Russian forces are on the other and all the roads out are too dangerous.
However, no breaches of the truce that began early on Tuesday have so far been reported.
US First Lady Melania Trump, who helped broker the ceasefire along with Pope Leo XIV, said on Tuesday that the area involved had been expanded to provide "safe passage" for humanitarian convoys.
Figure caption, What we know about Ukraine-Russia truce in Oleshky, brokered by Melania Trump
That was later corroborated by the press secretary to Ukraine's public ombudsman, and by Oleksandr Tolokonnikov, deputy head of Kherson, who said Russian shelling had stopped both in Kherson city, which is in Ukrainian hands, and the wider region.
Under the deal, the ceasefire will be followed by deliveries of humanitarian aid to Oleshky and then evacuations, planned for Friday, for anyone wishing to leave.
An estimated 1,700 to 2,000 people remain in Oleshky itself and a few thousand more in surrounding areas.
Many residents have resorted to cooking garden weeds to survive, telling the BBC they are suffering extreme hunger and want to leave.
Both sides said the ceasefire was being observed. Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said everything was proceeding "according to plan", and paid tribute to US mediation and in particular representatives of Melania Trump.
Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha said if the ceasefire produced results, it could "pave the way for other steps in the peace process".
A key official in President Volodymyr Zelensky's parliamentary party, David Arakhamia, said it would continue until 22:59 Ukrainian time on Sunday 1 November, and described the truce as the "largest de-escalation since 2022".
Before the war Oleshky was home to 24,000 people, but it was seized by Russia during the first days of its full-scale invasion in February 2022.
No shops are open, and the city has had no electricity, gas or water since the Kakhovka Dam was blown up in 2023, flooding the area and killing many people in Oleshky itself.
Conditions have become so desperate that not only is getting supplies into the city extremely difficult, but escaping is too risky because the routes out of Oleshky have been mined and subject to drone attack.
One woman told the BBC she had stepped on a landmine and was currently in hospital where she had undergone two operations: "I don't know how long I will have to spend there," she said, worried about not being able to join the evacuation.
Pope Leo appealed earlier this month to Russia's President Vladimir Putin to allow food and medical aid into Oleshky as well as a safe evacuation, and urged his Ukrainian counterpart Volodymyr Zelensky to co-operate with Moscow over a ceasefire.
Then the White House said last week that Melania Trump had secured a ceasefire.
On Tuesday, the US first lady said on X that the area covered by the ceasefire "has expanded beyond Oleshky, within the Kherson region, to provide safe passage for the humanitarian convoys".
Image caption, These residents were able to get out of Oleshky in spring this year
The current truce is supposed to enable roads to be cleared of mines for supplies to get into the city possibly on Thursday, and for residents to have safe passage out in an evacuation planned for Friday.
Russia's defence ministry said units from the army's Dnepr group had been conducting "engineering reconnaissance" and clearing main access roads into the village of "explosive and booby-trap devices".
Many details on the evacuation plans are unclear, and residents are wary of trusting officials with their names and addresses. However, a local volunteer told the BBC that about 500 people had already expressed interest by Tuesday afternoon.
Vladimir Saldo, the Russian-installed head of occupied areas of Kherson, said temporary accommodation had been prepared in the region itself as well as Russian-annexed Crimea and across the Russian border in the Rostov, Krasnodar and Stavropol regions.
Saldo told Russian media that most Oleshky residents wanted to leave the city and stay in Russia, although his account has not been corroborated on the ground.
Image caption, Oleshky has been under Russian occupation since 2022 and its people are now trapped
It is hard to make contact with people there as communication is patchy and many are reluctant to speak of the situation in fear of reprisals from the Russians.
Those residents or relatives who have spoken to the BBC have expressed fears that Russia may not allow them to return to Ukraine, or might examine their phones and online activity for signs of Ukrainian support, which could put them in danger.
Ukraine's military general staff urged people not to trust unverified reports or spread rumours about "the routes, time and place of the movement of people and humanitarian convoys".
White House says Melania Trump brokered truce for Ukraine city 'on brink of disaster'
Eating garden weeds to survive in Russian-occupied city cut off from food and water
To stay or risk the 'Road of Death' - Ukrainian civilians trapped in frontline city
Zelensky has warned that routes out of Oleshky that are demined by Russia will ensure that those civilians leaving Oleshky will "head towards Russia and stay there".
He said some residents would get to Ukrainian-controlled territory "one way or another", and that ideally anyone trapped would be able to reach their destination and evacuate to Ukraine.
One resident called Serhii, who fled Oleshky through minefields around three weeks ago, said he had eventually returned to Ukraine via Russia and Belarus. He called for a route across the River Dnipro that avoided Russian-occupied territory, saying "you simply cannot trust the Russian Federation".
However, bridges across the River Dnipro have been destroyed and sources say the riverbank is also mined and dangerous, so crossing into Ukrainian-controlled territory appears impossible.
Across the river, in Kherson city, no explosions have been heard and no drone-related injuries reported since 03:00 (01:00 GMT) on Tuesday and cars and pedestrians have been moving freely, according to local reports.
"Judging from the fact that more people are walking around, it feels a bit calmer," Galina Kyrychenko, a resident in the city, told public broadcaster Suspilne.

items.content:
Russia is advancing legislation that would allow vehicles reported stolen in Europe, Canada, and Ukraine to be registered legally in Russia, even if they remain on Interpol’s international wanted list.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
According to Russian media Kommersant on October 28, the Russian State Duma’s Transport Committee recommended that lawmakers approve a bill drafted by the Interior Ministry in its first reading. The proposal would establish special registration procedures for vehicles wanted by law enforcement agencies in countries Moscow officially classifies as “unfriendly.”
Deputy Interior Minister Igor Zubov told lawmakers that the proposed changes were partly driven by Russia’s war against Ukraine.
Category Latest news Russia May Grant Legal Registration to Smuggled Cars Stolen Across Europe
He explained that Russian authorities in occupied Ukrainian territories have encountered difficulties registering vehicles previously registered in Ukraine because Ukrainian law enforcement agencies had placed them on Interpol’s wanted list.
Under existing Russian regulations, vehicles subject to international search notices cannot be registered, even if they have already entered Russian territory. Zubov described the proposed legislation as a temporary solution intended to prevent such vehicles from remaining unused.
The Interior Ministry prepared the proposal in February 2026, and the Russian government subsequently submitted it to the State Duma in June. The initiative follows a separate ruling by Russia’s Supreme Court involving a St. Petersburg resident who purchased a vehicle stolen in Canada.
In October, the court sided with the buyer after Russian traffic police refused to register the vehicle because of its international wanted status. The ruling was presented as protecting buyers who had purchased imported vehicles in good faith.
According to  The Moscow Times on October 28, Russia has become a major destination for vehicles stolen in Europe and North America since the beginning of its full-scale invasion of Ukraine and the introduction of Western sanctions.
Category Latest news Stolen EU Vehicles Reappear in Russia With “Clean” Papers After Donbas Detour
Between February 2024 and July 2026, Interpol recorded 4,798 reports involving vehicles stolen in Canada that were subsequently operated in Russia, the outlet reported.
Thousands of additional imported vehicles entering Russia through parallel import channels, including routes through the United Arab Emirates, have also reportedly appeared in international stolen-vehicle databases.
During the early months of Russia’s full-scale invasion in 2022, Russian troops seized civilian vehicles from occupied Ukrainian territories, with some later spotted in Belarus without license plates and bearing Russian military “V” markings.
The United Nations also documented Russian forces confiscating vehicles from private homes, businesses, and civilians at checkpoints for military and personal use.

items.content:
OpenAI Reportedly Plans to Purchase Google AI Chips as Demand for Computing Infrastructure Grows
OpenAI (NASDAQ:OAI) is planning to purchase artificial intelligence chips developed by Alphabet's Google (NASDAQ:GOOG), according to a report published Tuesday by The Information, citing a person familiar with the matter. The potential agreement would expand the commercial relationship between the two companies as demand for AI computing infrastructure continues to increase.
The reported plans come as major technology companies commit substantial capital to data centres, processors and other infrastructure required to develop and operate advanced artificial intelligence models.
Financial terms and other details of the proposed purchases were not disclosed. Google did not immediately respond to a Reuters request for comment outside regular business hours, while OpenAI declined to comment.
The potential chip purchases would represent another development in the relationship between OpenAI and Google, which compete in artificial intelligence products and internet search.
Despite that competition, the companies have increasingly established commercial arrangements involving computing infrastructure and AI services.
Last week, OpenAI announced that it would make its frontier artificial intelligence models available through Google Cloud.
The agreement provides another distribution channel for OpenAI's advanced models while expanding the range of AI services available through Google's cloud platform.
The reported plan to purchase Google-designed chips would extend the relationship into semiconductor procurement.
However, neither company has confirmed the proposed transaction, and the report did not specify purchase volumes, pricing or delivery schedules.
Google's Tensor Processing Units, or TPUs, have gained attention as an alternative to the graphics processing units supplied by Nvidia.
TPUs are specialized processors designed to handle computational workloads associated with artificial intelligence, including model training and inference.
OpenAI is already one of the largest purchasers of Nvidia GPUs, which it uses to develop and deploy its AI systems.
The company has also previously accessed Google's semiconductor technology.
Reuters reported in June 2025 that OpenAI had begun renting Google's AI chips, establishing an earlier commercial relationship involving the processors.
The latest report suggests OpenAI is considering direct purchases rather than relying exclusively on rented computing capacity.
Google began selling TPUs directly to selected customers this year as demand for alternatives to Nvidia's processors increased.
The reported transaction comes amid substantial investment in the infrastructure required to support artificial intelligence development.
Amazon, Microsoft and Alphabet expect to spend as much as $600 billion collectively this year on AI-related infrastructure.
The spending includes investments in data centres, computing equipment and systems needed to operate increasingly complex AI models.
As capital expenditure rises, investors are paying closer attention to the financial returns generated by these investments.
Companies developing AI systems are also evaluating different semiconductor technologies as they seek to manage computing costs and secure sufficient processing capacity.
Google's TPUs have attracted interest partly because they offer another option alongside Nvidia's widely used GPUs.
For OpenAI, access to additional chip suppliers could broaden the range of hardware available for its computing requirements.
Alphabet Earnings Expected to Provide AI Infrastructure Update
Alphabet is scheduled to report its quarterly financial results later on Wednesday.
Investors will examine the performance of Google Cloud and the company's spending on artificial intelligence infrastructure.
The results are expected to provide further information about whether demand for AI services and computing capacity is translating into revenue growth.
Google's TPU business has benefited from commercial agreements with customers, including OpenAI rival Anthropic.
These arrangements have contributed to demand for Google's proprietary semiconductor technology.
Alphabet Chief Financial Officer Anat Ashkenazi previously indicated that the company expects to recognize a small percentage of revenue associated with TPU sales agreements by the end of 2026.
The majority of revenue from those agreements is expected to be recognized during 2027.
The timing reflects the longer-term nature of some semiconductor supply arrangements and the period over which contracted sales are expected to contribute to Alphabet's financial results.
Alongside its reported interest in Google's chips, OpenAI is developing its own semiconductor technology.
In June, the company unveiled its first custom artificial intelligence chip, designed in collaboration with Broadcom.
OpenAI said it planned to deploy the processor by the end of 2026 as part of a multigeneration chip development programme.
The initiative represents another approach to securing the computing capacity required for the company's AI models.
Developing proprietary processors could allow OpenAI to tailor hardware to its specific computing requirements while continuing to use chips supplied by external manufacturers.
The programme also demonstrates the range of semiconductor procurement and development strategies being pursued by major AI companies.
Competition and Commercial Partnerships Continue Across AI Industry
The reported chip purchases illustrate how companies competing in artificial intelligence can also maintain commercial relationships.
Google and OpenAI compete in areas including generative AI models, consumer applications and search-related services.
At the same time, Google Cloud provides computing infrastructure that can support the deployment of OpenAI models.
A direct chip supply arrangement would create another commercial connection between the companies.
The development also reflects the growing importance of semiconductor availability in determining how quickly AI developers can expand their computing operations.
Nvidia remains a major supplier of AI processors, but Google's TPU sales and custom chip programmes involving companies such as Broadcom demonstrate efforts to diversify hardware options.
OpenAI's reported plan to purchase Google's AI chips would expand an existing commercial relationship that already includes access to Google Cloud services and previously reported TPU rentals.
The proposed transaction has not been confirmed, and no financial terms or purchase volumes have been disclosed.
For Google, direct TPU sales represent an additional opportunity to generate revenue from its semiconductor technology alongside its cloud computing business.
Alphabet expects most revenue from existing TPU sales agreements to be recognized in 2027, with a smaller contribution anticipated before the end of 2026.
Meanwhile, OpenAI is continuing its custom chip development programme with Broadcom, with initial deployment planned before year-end.
The developments highlight the increasing importance of semiconductor supply, computing costs and infrastructure investment as artificial intelligence companies expand their operations.

items.title: China's families are now supporting more old people than kids
items.summary: The latest figures mark a major milestone as Beijing grapples with an ageing population.
items.content:
Families in China are for the first time supporting more elderly people than children, the country's government has said.
Official data released in the last week , external show the ratio of China's dependent elderly people compared to the working age population rose to 23% last year, overtaking the figure for children, which stood at 22%.
The numbers are closely watched for signs of how China's shrinking workforce will impact both the world's second largest economy and global growth as a whole.
The latest figures mark a significant milestone as China grapples with an ageing population that could have implications for families, pensions and healthcare spending, analysts say.
China has been preparing for a growing proportion of elderly people in recent years, while urging younger generations to get married and for couples to have more children .
The latest data from China's National Bureau of Statistics show there are now more than 223 million people in China aged 65 and above, accounting for nearly 16% of the country's total population.
At the same time there are about 213 million children aged 14 and under.
No official commentary was published with the statistics. But Chinese state-controlled news outlet Global Times wrote that the nation's "entry into a moderately ageing society" is the result of a mix of factors, including the "size of past birth cohorts" and longer life expectancy.
The shift could place added strain on pension, healthcare and long-term care systems, while also creating opportunities in the so-called silver economy that caters to older consumers, the newspaper said.
"It reflects a historical trend in demographic development rather than a short-term phenomenon," Global Times quoted one researcher as saying.
The demographic shift is "symbolic" and could suggest more public spending will move from families and schools to pensions and healthcare, said Professor Stuart Gietel-Basten from The Hong Kong University of Science and Technology.
It may also pose a challenge to the country's ambitions, as it could limit its economic growth as well as people's spending power, said National University of Singapore sociology lecturer Mu Zheng.
Image caption, Birth rates in China have been falling for years now
China's ageing population has been driven by a mix of factors, including rapid urbanisation and the effects of the controversial one-child policy , which was in place from 1980 to the end of 2015.
The strategy, designed to keep China's rapid population growth under control, is estimated by the country's government to have prevented about 400 million births since it began, though this number has been contested.
The policy played a key role in shrinking the population and means there are fewer younger people to support a growing number of elderly relatives, Mu said.
But despite easing restrictions on the size of families, Beijing has struggled to persuade couples to have more children, with birth rates hitting historic lows.
Other contributing factors include changing gender roles, rising living costs and higher education levels that have put pressure on fertility rates, Mu said.
Beijing made further support for older people a part of the measures in its five-year economic blueprint that was announced earlier this year.
Financial help for pensioners has been a growing part of Chinese government spending. More than 53 million elderly people were receiving senior citizen allowances and subsidies by the end of 2025, according to official figures.
The Global Times noted that many people entering old age who were born between the 1950s and the 1970s have generally higher incomes compared to previous generations, stronger purchasing power and are healthier.
The dependency ratio is widely-used to measure ageing populations but it has also been questioned by some experts who argue that its scope is too limited.
Gietel-Basten said the use of the statistics risks "taking agency away" from older people - many of whom he says have been misrepresented as dependants.
It also does not take into account improvements to healthcare, he added.

items.title: In Serbia, a new type of democracy is taking hold, and Europe is watching closely
items.summary: A movement that began in outrage has delivered remarkable election upset, showing that change is possible and prompting questions over what comes next• Don’t get This Is Europe delivered to your inbox? Sign up hereIn April of last year, dozens of students set off from Serbia, intent on making it to Strasbourg, France on bicycles. The
items.content:
As people celebrate in Serbia, the rest of Europe is ready for change. Photograph: Marko Drobnjaković/AP
As people celebrate in Serbia, the rest of Europe is ready for change. Photograph: Marko Drobnjaković/AP
In Serbia, a new type of democracy is taking hold, and Europe is watching closely
A movement that began in outrage has delivered remarkable election upset, showing that change is possible and prompting questions over what comes next
Don’t get This Is Europe delivered to your inbox? Sign up here
I n April of last year, dozens of students set off from Serbia , intent on making it to Strasbourg, France on bicycles. The aim of the arduous, 13-day transcontinental journey was simple: to make their voices heard in Europe and beyond.
In their home city of Novi Sad, students had been holding near-daily protests after a deadly roof collapse at the city’s main railway station. As their push for accountability and justice spread across the country, it was met with baton-wielding police, teargas and a political class that branded these young people as traitors.
Their trek to Strasbourg was aimed at casting a spotlight on the deepening erosion of democratic values in their home country. “Serbia needs Europe’s support,” the students explained in an open letter to the French president, Emmanuel Macron, as they arrived in Strasbourg and met with MEPs and officials. “We are not riding toward Europe to flee Serbia. We are riding to bring it back.”
On Sunday, their movement made headlines across the world as the students were catapulted from the streets of Serbia into the halls of power. In a ballot that saw the highest turnout since the breakup of Yugoslavia in 1992, over 50% of voters backed the students to oust the increasingly authoritarian leader, Aleksandar Vučić, and end his party’s 14 years in power.
It was, as a Guardian editorial noted, “one of the most remarkable election outcomes in recent European history”.
The students’ extraordinary feat came as Europe has been rocked by weeks of protests. From Porto to Paris and Madrid to Milan, analysts have pointed to the common thread that weaves through the diverse protests: a view that the social contract has broken down, leaving younger generations bracing for a future in which they will be worse off than their parents.
The election result in Serbia lays bare the power of these protests to reshape politics, postdoctoral researcher Aleksandar Matković noted this week . Could it be, as WikiLeaks founder Julian Assange once told an interviewer in Belgrade, that Serbia is “a country where the future happens first”?
Matković drew on his involvement inside the student movement to offer a singular window into all that had gone into their win, citing discussions that had stretched as long as six hours as the students laid the groundwork for their entry into politics. “The world should be watching closely: it may be witnessing the start of a very different kind of politics,” he wrote.
Their win sparked joy across Serbia, sending tens of thousands of jubilant revelers on to streets across the country. “It’s very strange that on the very streets where the police beat us, on the streets where we retreated countless times in the face of the gendarmerie, we are now standing here as the victors,” Sara, 24, told the Guardian.
Hours later supporters of the movement appeared again, this time to clean up after a night of raucous celebrations.
When the celebrations are over, the question of government begins. Photograph: Aleksandar Jovicic/NurPhoto/Shutterstock The movement now faces a tremendous task – particularly given that it has no hierarchy or leader. For more than a decade, Vučić’s party had transformed the state, tightening its grip on media, stuffing institutions with loyalists to the party and wielding ministries and Serbian institutions as political tools.
The movement won 140 of the 250 seats in parliament, giving a comfortable majority to a slate of candidates who range from academics to athletes, and who were chosen via student assemblies in the lead-up to the election. As one candidate told my colleagues on Monday, the top priority was “the social and psychological detoxification” of the country.
Underpinning the movement is an 11-point plan, which includes ridding the country of corruption, reforming the judiciary and media and improving access to healthcare. “We are neither promising, nor expecting overnight miracles as a result of this victory,” one member of the movement wrote in the Guardian this week. “Rather we hope for something fundamentally radical for Serbia: normal, functioning institutions.”
And while their plans for power take shape, the impact of their bold experiment will certainly be felt far beyond Serbia. The country applied to join the European Union in 2009, but the process has largely stalled in recent years. Now, much like in neighbouring Hungary, the elections have ushered in the possibility of a fresh start along with hope of a democratic resurgence in central Europe.
As EU officials sent their congratulations this week to the students, whose policy platform promises to put the question of future EU membership to a referendum, a note of optimism laced their messages. “We stand ready to support reforms on the rule of law, media freedom, the fight against corruption and strong democratic institutions and to work together to advance Serbia’s future in the European Union,” the European Commission chief, Ursula von der Leyen, said on social media.
Marta Kos, the EU’s enlargement commissioner, was more direct. “A new chapter can begin for Serbia. The door to the EU is open, and we are ready to move forward together,” she wrote on social media.
It was a stunning reversal of fortunes for the students who last year felt they had to cycle more than 1,300km (780 miles) to make their voices heard. Now – after nearly two years of protests that were met with detentions on trumped-up evidence, illegal surveillance, threats and job losses – it seems they might have a chance to fulfil their wish of bringing Europe to Serbia.

items.title: Gulf states working on multipart peace deal to avert renewal of US-Iran war - The Guardian
items.summary: Gulf states working on multipart peace deal to avert renewal of US-Iran war  The Guardian
items.content:
Iran wants guarantees of sanctions relief in return for reopening the strait of Hormuz. Photograph: Amirhosein Khorgooi/AP
Iran wants guarantees of sanctions relief in return for reopening the strait of Hormuz. Photograph: Amirhosein Khorgooi/AP
Gulf states working on multipart peace deal to avert renewal of US-Iran war
Talks are aimed at reopening strait of Hormuz and lifting sanctions on Iran, and for Houthis to withdraw in Yemen
A multipronged peace deal to reopen the strait of Hormuz within four days of sanctions being lifted and for the Houthis to withdraw substantial forces inside Yemen are at the heart of Gulf states’ plans to avert what they regard as a disastrous renewal of war between Iran and the US.
The US is aware of the talks’ progress but is holding out for a concession that European powers suggest could involve Iran allowing UN weapons inspectors back into the country.
The British foreign secretary, Ed Miliband, urged the Iranians to agree to readmit the UN weapons inspectors when he met the Iranian foreign minister, Abbas Araghchi, in New York but so far Iran has refused, saying it will only hold talks in principle on its nuclear programme.
Oil price rises above $117 a barrel amid fears US will renew strikes on Iran
European diplomats believe allowing weapons inspectors to reenter Iran and visit its bombed nuclear sites is a minimum requirement for a breakthrough with the US president, Donald Trump.
But Iran remains focused solely on the guarantees of sanctions relief it would receive in return for reopening the strait of Hormuz . Dr Ali Bagheri, the deputy secretary of Iran’s national security council, said Iran was willing to reduce its proposal that the strait reopen seven days after economic sanctions are lifted to four days.
In a further sign of flexibility, Iran is starting to acknowledge it has a mediating role in the parallel conflict in Yemen . Iran’s secretary of the supreme national security council, Mohsen Rezaei, met the Houthi’s ambassador to Iran, Ibrahim al-Dulaimi, on Tuesday.
The meeting took place 24 hours after a high-level delegation from Saudi Arabia, Turkey and Pakistan travelled to Tehran to discuss Saudi terms for ending the Yemen conflict as well as a longer-term security architecture for the region.
Iran backs the Houthis, and has the power to influence them, including devising proposals that stop short of a Houthi military victory that many say is unobtainable. In return the Houthis are demanding that Saudi Arabia lift what it regards as a naval and air blockade on Houthi-held territory.
Iran successfully prevented discussion of its nuclear programme at the meeting with Turkey, Saudi Arabia and Pakistan, and instead ensured the focus was a broader discussion about a long-term regional security vision that would include the Gulf states and Iran and see the US presence in the Middle East reduced or ended.
A new non-aggression pact in which Iran is no longer ostracised by the rest of the Gulf, as it has been since the 1979 Islamic Revolution, would meet Iran’s highest strategic goal.
An agreed commitment to this goal by six Gulf states might also make it easier for Iran to swallow potentially difficult tactical concessions that it would be required to make concerning its nuclear programme.
US and Israel are warned against launching fresh strikes on Iran
One of the key advocates of the inclusive security plan, Oman’s foreign minister, Badr Albusaidi , said he believed the US administration understood this was the direction the region is heading.
He said: “I think if Iran is fully re-engaged in this idea of having all of us, eight countries at peace with the rest of the world, the economic potential is going to be enormous for all of us in the region and those outside the region who choose to take part in this development. We have really discussed this in at length during the talks between Iran and the United States, and I think there is general acceptance that this will be the direction of travel once we have a deal in place at the end of the day.”
At a televised event in Iran this week Araghchi underlined the importance of a new postwar security pact to Iran, saying: “Recently, there has been talk of a new war but I am already thinking about the postwar period. Whether there is war or not, our policies remain the same.”

items.title: Iran rejects 'unacceptable' proposal by Qatar to end war with US - Middle East Eye
items.summary: Iran rejects 'unacceptable' proposal by Qatar to end war with US  Middle East Eye
items.content:
Iran has rejected a proposal from Qatar to end the US -led war on the country, calling it "unacceptable".
Qatar presented the draft deal, which would look to end the eight-month conflict, to Iranian negotiators on Sunday.
However, a senior Iranian official told Reuters on Wednesday that his country could not work with what had been presented, adding that Tehran would show no flexibility regarding the nuclear issue.
US Vice President JD Vance said earlier this month that Iran must reduce nuclear enrichment to end the war. The Islamic Republic has repeatedly stated that its nuclear programme is entirely for non-military domestic use.
The negotiations come amid mounting fears that the US and Israel could imminently resume their attacks on Iran.
Israel-Palestine, alongside Turkey Unpacked and other MEE newsletters
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, in particular, has been touting the prospect of new attacks as he seeks re-election in Israel's parliamentary elections .
With 77 percent of votes counted, Netanyahu's bloc is the largest in the Israeli parliament.
On Wednesday, as negotiations were set to begin on forming a new government, Netanyahu announced he would work with US President Donald Trump to eliminate the "existential threat" posed by Iran.
His main rival, Gadi Eisenkot, has also supported strikes on Iran in tandem with economic pressure.
The Israel-US war on Iran has, since it began in February, caused massive disruption to the global economy, sending energy prices soaring.
Iran's Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi warned on Wednesday that any Israeli-instigated attack in the Gulf region would have a "devastating impact" on global markets.
"Devastating impact on int'l markets of any Israel-instigated military misadventure in Persian Gulf region remains major concern for both gas suppliers and consumers," Araghchi said in a post on X.
'Escalation is coming': Middle East on edge as new Israeli-US attack on Iran looms
The fallout of any renewed conflict in the Gulf would also be compounded by the ongoing fighting between Saudi Arabia and the Iran-aligned Houthis in Yemen .
The Houthis, officially named Ansar Allah, on Wednesday called for the evacuation of the airport in Aden, the city in southern Yemen that serves as the seat of the Saudi-backed government.
"Our armed forces call on those present at Aden Airport to evacuate the premises immediately, due to the presence of a Saudi military cargo plane carrying weapons intended to kill the Yemeni people," Houthi spokesperson Yahya Saree wrote on X.
Fighting between the Houthis and Saudi-backed forces in Yemen has seen nearly 100 fighters killed since Monday, military sources from both sides told AFP.
At least 63 Houthi fighters and 34 combatants associated with the internationally recognised government died, mostly near the Bab al-Mandab Strait.
